facts: Allhallows-on-Sea was planned as a major seaside resort in the 1930s but never fully developed.
The village sits on the Hoo Peninsula, looking out over the Thames Estuary.
Its holiday park remains a popular caravan and camping destination today.
Capstone Farm Country Park covers over 100 hectares of Kent countryside near Chatham.
The park includes a lake, woodland and grazing meadows.
It was created from former farmland to provide green space for the growing Medway towns.
Chatham Dockyard built and repaired Royal Navy ships for over 400 years, closing in 1984.
It preserves the world's most complete dockyard from the age of sail.
HMS Victory's timbers were partly sourced from Chatham's associated forests.
Cliffe Pools is a major RSPB reserve created from former flooded chalk and clay pits.
It attracts large numbers of wading birds and wildfowl on the Hoo Peninsula.
The site sits close to the marshes that inspired the opening of Dickens' Great Expectations.
Fort Amherst is Britain's largest Napoleonic-era fortification, built to defend Chatham Dockyard.
It includes a network of tunnels dug into the chalk beneath the fort.
The fort dates from the 1750s, with later Napoleonic-era additions.
Gillingham Strand is a stretch of Medway riverside promenade and green space.
It offers views across the River Medway towards Hoo.
The Strand sits close to the historic naval town of Gillingham.
Gravesend Town Pier, opened in 1834, is the oldest surviving cast-iron pier in the world.
It once served as a landing stage for Thames steamers bringing day-trippers from London.
The pier has been restored and now houses a bar and restaurant.
The Hoo Peninsula sits between the Thames and Medway estuaries.
It is largely low-lying marshland, historically used for grazing and, in Dickens' time, as smugglers' territory.
Plans to build a major airport on the peninsula were rejected in 2010.
The Isle of Grain sits at the tip of the Hoo Peninsula, where the Thames meets the Medway.
It has long been an important site for oil refining and, more recently, gas storage.
Despite its name, the Isle of Grain has been connected to the mainland by land reclamation for centuries.
Joss Bay is a popular sandy beach near Broadstairs, known for surfing.
It sits along the chalk cliffs of the Isle of Thanet.
The bay's name is thought to derive from a historic shipwreck or smuggling connection.
Margate's harbour has been a working port since medieval times.
The town's Turner Contemporary gallery, named after painter J.M.W. Turner, opened on the harbour arm in 2011.
Margate's Old Town retains narrow medieval streets close to the harbour.
The Medway Tunnel, opened in 1996, carries road traffic beneath the River Medway.
It was the first purpose-built immersed tube tunnel constructed in the UK for road use.
The tunnel links Chatham and Strood, reducing pressure on the historic Rochester bridge.
Minnis Bay is a sandy beach at Birchington-on-Sea, popular for watersports.
The bay has a long tradition of sailing and windsurfing clubs.
Birchington sits on the north Kent coast, part of the Isle of Thanet.
North Foreland Lighthouse is one of the last lighthouses in England to be automated, in 1998.
It marks the point where the Thames Estuary meets the open North Sea.
The current tower dates largely from the 17th and 18th centuries.
Palm Bay is a quieter sandy beach on the northeast Kent coast near Margate.
It sits beneath low chalk cliffs typical of the Thanet coastline.
The bay is a popular spot for rock pooling at low tide.
Pegwell Bay is a large tidal bay and nature reserve on the Kent coast.
A full-size replica Viking longship, the Hugin, commemorates the traditional 449 AD landing of Hengist and Horsa nearby.
The bay is an important habitat for wading birds.
Rainham, Kent, has a history stretching back to Anglo-Saxon times, distinct from the London borough of the same name.
The town's parish church, St Margaret's, has origins dating to the 12th century.
Rainham sits between Gillingham and Sittingbourne on the North Kent coast line.
Ramsgate's harbour is the only Royal Harbour in the UK, a title granted by George IV in 1821.
The town played a key role during the 1940 Dunkirk evacuation, with many 'Little Ships' departing from its harbour.
Ramsgate's Georgian architecture reflects its heyday as a fashionable seaside resort.
Rochester Cathedral is the second-oldest cathedral in England, founded in 604 AD.
Charles Dickens lived nearby and set scenes from several novels in the city.
The cathedral's crypt is one of the largest and finest Norman crypts in the country.
St Mary's Island, near Chatham, was developed on former dockyard land into a modern residential district.
It sits on the River Medway, connected to the mainland by a causeway.
The island takes its name from an earlier, smaller island absorbed into the dockyard site.
Stone Bay is a quiet beach near Broadstairs on the Thanet coast.
It sits between the busier bays of Broadstairs and Ramsgate.
The bay is popular with local residents away from the main tourist crowds.
Tilbury Fort is one of the finest surviving examples of 17th-century military engineering in England.
Elizabeth I delivered her famous Armada speech to troops gathered near the fort in 1588.
It later served coastal defence roles into the 20th century.
Upchurch Marshes line the Medway estuary, historically used for grazing and brick-making clay extraction.
The area has yielded significant Roman pottery finds from ancient kiln sites.
Upchurch village sits a short distance inland from the marshes.
Viking Bay is Broadstairs' main beach, sheltered by chalk headlands either side.
Charles Dickens holidayed frequently in Broadstairs, and Bleak House overlooks the bay.
The bay hosts the town's popular annual Dickens Festival.
Westgate-on-Sea developed as a deliberately quiet, upmarket Victorian resort.
The town has two sandy bays either side of its centre.
Westgate was designed with wide streets and large villas to attract wealthy residents.
Canterbury Cathedral is the mother church of the worldwide Anglican Communion.
Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered inside the cathedral in 1170.
The cathedral is a UNESCO World Heritage Site along with St Augustine's Abbey and St Martin's Church.
Dover Castle is often called the 'Key to England' for its strategic position guarding the shortest Channel crossing.
Secret wartime tunnels beneath the castle were used to plan the 1940 Dunkirk evacuation.
The castle's Great Tower was built by Henry II in the 1180s.
Leeds Castle sits on two islands in a lake, often called 'the loveliest castle in the world'.
It has served as a Norman stronghold, a royal residence, and a private country house over its history.
Bearsted is the nearest railway station, with the castle reached by road or seasonal bus.
Sissinghurst's garden was created in the 1930s by writer Vita Sackville-West and her husband Harold Nicolson.
It is considered one of the most influential gardens of the 20th century.
Staplehurst is the nearest railway station on the Hastings line.
Knole is one of England's largest houses, said to have 365 rooms, one for each day of the year.
It has been the ancestral home of the Sackville family since the 16th century.
Knole Park, surrounding the house, is home to free-roaming deer.
The Pantiles is a colonnaded Georgian parade built around the town's mineral spring.
Tunbridge Wells was granted 'Royal' status by Edward VII in 1909.
The spa town developed after the spring's medicinal waters were discovered in 1606.
Rye's cobbled Mermaid Street is one of the most photographed streets in England.
The town was once a leading member of the Cinque Ports confederation, though the sea has since receded.
Rye sits on a hill that was once nearly surrounded by water.
Battle Abbey was built by William the Conqueror on the site of the 1066 Battle of Hastings.
The high altar was said to mark the spot where King Harold fell.
The town of Battle grew up around the abbey to house its workers.
Hastings Castle was the first castle built by William the Conqueror in England, in 1066.
The town's Old Town retains narrow medieval streets and traditional net shops for fishing gear.
Hastings remains a working fishing beach, one of the largest in Europe launched directly from the shore.
Whitstable has been famous for oyster farming since Roman times.
The town hosts an annual Oyster Festival each July.
Whitstable's fishing harbour and weatherboarded houses give it a distinctive character.
Deal Castle was built by Henry VIII in a distinctive Tudor rose shape for coastal defence.
It was part of a chain of forts built to defend against invasion after Henry's break with Rome.
Deal has one of the best-preserved seafronts of its kind on the Kent coast.
Walmer Castle has been the official residence of the Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports for centuries.
The Duke of Wellington died at Walmer Castle in 1852 while serving as Lord Warden.
The castle's gardens include one planted specially for the Queen Mother.
Sandwich was one of the original Cinque Ports, medieval towns granted privileges for providing ships to the crown.
The Earl of Sandwich, linked to the food's name, took his title from the town.
Sandwich's medieval street plan survives almost entirely intact.
Faversham is home to Britain's oldest brewer, Shepherd Neame, established in 1698.
The town has one of the largest collections of listed buildings in England for its size.
Faversham was once one of England's most important market towns.
Bodiam Castle is one of the most complete and picturesque moated castles in England, built in 1385.
It was constructed to defend against a feared French invasion during the Hundred Years' War.
Robertsbridge is the nearest railway station, connecting to the castle via the Kent and East Sussex Railway.
Chartwell was Sir Winston Churchill's family home for over 40 years.
Churchill painted many works in the garden studio, several still on display.
The house is now cared for by the National Trust.
Groombridge Place is a moated 17th-century manor house on the Kent-Sussex border.
Its gardens include a themed 'Enchanted Forest' woodland walk.
Frant is the nearest railway station on the Hastings line.
Penshurst Place is one of the best-preserved medieval manor houses in England.
It has been the ancestral home of the Sidney family since the 16th century.
Tonbridge is the nearest mainline station, with the house reached by road.
Tonbridge Castle's motte-and-bailey design dates from shortly after the Norman Conquest.
The gatehouse, added in the 13th century, is one of the best-preserved in England.
Tonbridge sits on the River Medway, a key crossing point historically.
Ightham Mote is a moated medieval manor house dating largely from the 14th century.
It is considered one of the finest examples of its kind in England.
Borough Green & Wrotham is the nearest railway station, with the house reached by road.
The Archbishop's Palace in Maidstone was once a residence for the Archbishops of Canterbury.
Maidstone is the county town of Kent.
The town sits on the River Medway, historically an important trading route.
Charles Dickens spent much of his childhood in the Medway towns, later drawing on the area in his novels.
Chatham developed largely around its historic naval dockyard.
The town remains one of the Medway 'Towns', alongside Rochester and Gillingham.
Sittingbourne was historically a major centre of paper manufacturing.
The town is linked to the heritage Sittingbourne and Kemsley Light Railway, once used to move paper stock.
Sittingbourne sits on Milton Creek, a tidal inlet of the Swale.
Herne Bay's clock tower, built in 1837, is thought to be the first purpose-built free-standing clock tower in the world.
The town once had one of the longest pleasure piers in England, though much was lost to storms.
Herne Bay developed as a Victorian seaside resort.
Bleak House overlooks Viking Bay, named after Charles Dickens' novel written partly nearby.
Dickens holidayed in Broadstairs regularly for over 20 years.
The town holds an annual Dickens Festival celebrating this connection.
Ashford International was built to serve Eurostar services on the Channel Tunnel Rail Link.
The station remains a key gateway between Kent and mainland Europe for freight and passenger rail.
Ashford has been an important railway town since the 1840s, once home to major locomotive works.
